msg.content:
<document>
<title>Bordeaux wine</title>
<fragment>
* *Red Libourne, or "Right Bank" wines*. Around the city of Libourne, 10 appellations produce wines dominated by Merlot with very little Cabernet Sauvignon, the two most famous being Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. These wines often have great fruit concentration, softer tannins and are long-lived. Saint-Émilion has an official classification.[20] In 2007, 10.5% of the region's vineyard surface was used for wines in this family.[17]
* *Red Graves and Médoc or "Left Bank" wines*. North and south of the city of Bordeaux, which are the classic areas, produce wines dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, but often with a significant portion of Merlot. These wines are concentrated, tannic, long-lived and most of them meant to be cellared before drinking. The five First Growths are situated here. There are official classifications for both Médoc and Graves.[21] In 2007, 17.1% of the region's vineyard surface was used for wines in this family.[17]

</fragment>
<fragment>
New reforms for the regional appellations were instituted in 2008 by the Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur Winemakers' Association. In 2010, 55% of all Bordeaux wines sold in the world were from Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur AOCs, with 67% sold in France and 33% exported (+9%), representing 14 bottles consumed per second.[17][18]
* *Red Côtes de Bordeaux*. Eight appellations are in the hilly outskirts of the region, and produce wines where the blend usually is dominated by Merlot. These wines tend to be intermediate between basic red Bordeaux and the more famous appellations of the left and right bank in both style and quality. However, since none of Bordeaux's stellar names are situated in Côtes de Bordeaux, prices tend to be moderate. There is no official classification in Côtes de Bordeaux.[19] In 2007, 14.7% of the region's vineyard surface was used for wines in this family.[17]

</fragment>
<fragment>
There are four different classifications of Bordeaux, covering different parts of the region:[24]




</fragment>
<fragment>

As a broad generalisation, Cabernet Sauvignon (Bordeaux's second-most planted grape variety) dominates the blend in red wines produced in the Médoc and the rest of the left bank of the Gironde estuary. Typical top-quality Châteaux blends are 70% Cabernet Sauvignon, 15% Cabernet Franc and 15% Merlot. This is typically referred to as the "Bordeaux blend". Merlot tends to predominate in Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and the other right bank appellations. These Right Bank blends from top -quality Châteaux are typically 70% Merlot, 15% Cabernet Franc and 15% Cabernet Sauvignon.[16]



### Whites[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Average vintages produce over 700 million bottles of wine, ranging from large quantities of everyday table wine, to some of the most expensive and prestigious wines in the world. The vast majority of wine produced in Bordeaux is red (sometimes called "claret" in Britain), with sweet white wines (most notably Sauternes), dry whites, and (in much smaller quantities) rosé and sparkling wines (Crémant de Bordeaux) collectively making up the remainder. Bordeaux wine is made by more than 5,660 producers or *châteaux*. There are 65 appellations of Bordeaux wine.[2][3]




## History[edit]


![](image)Map of the French provinces (including Bordeaux) assimilated by the Plantagenet-Aquitaine union
Main article: History of Bordeaux wine

Viticulture was introduced into the Bordeaux region by the  Romans, probably in the mid-1st century CE,[4]
to provide wine for local consumption, and wine production has been continuous in the region since then.[5][*need quotation to verify*]


</fragment>
</document>

</fragment>
<fragment>
New reforms for the regional appellations were instituted in 2008 by the Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur Winemakers' Association. In 2010, 55% of all Bordeaux wines sold in the world were from Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur AOCs, with 67% sold in France and 33% exported (+9%), representing 14 bottles consumed per second.[17][18]
* *Red Côtes de Bordeaux*. Eight appellations are in the hilly outskirts of the region, and produce wines where the blend usually is dominated by Merlot. These wines tend to be intermediate between basic red Bordeaux and the more famous appellations of the left and right bank in both style and quality. However, since none of Bordeaux's stellar names are situated in Côtes de Bordeaux, prices tend to be moderate. There is no official classification in Côtes de Bordeaux.[19] In 2007, 14.7% of the region's vineyard surface was used for wines in this family.[17]

</fragment>
<fragment>

Average vintages produce over 700 million bottles of wine, ranging from large quantities of everyday table wine, to some of the most expensive and prestigious wines in the world. The vast majority of wine produced in Bordeaux is red (sometimes called "claret" in Britain), with sweet white wines (most notably Sauternes), dry whites, and (in much smaller quantities) rosé and sparkling wines (Crémant de Bordeaux) collectively making up the remainder. Bordeaux wine is made by more than 5,660 producers or *châteaux*. There are 65 appellations of Bordeaux wine.[2][3]

![](image)Map of the French provinces (including Bordeaux) assimilated by the Plantagenet-Aquitaine union

These wines often have great fruit concentration, softer tannins and are long-lived. Saint-Émilion has an official classification.[20] In 2007, 10.5% of the region's vineyard surface was used for wines in this family.[17]
* *Red Graves and Médoc or "Left Bank" wines*. North and south of the city of Bordeaux, which are the classic areas, produce wines dominated by Cabernet Sauvignon, but often with a significant portion of Merlot. These wines are concentrated, tannic, long-lived and most of them meant to be cellared before drinking. The five First Growths are situated here. **Bordeaux’s five most widely‑planted grape varieties (2022‑2023 vineyard‑area data)**  

| Rank | Grape variety | Approx. share of total Bordeaux vineyard * | Main sub‑region(s) where it is most heavily planted | Typical role in the blend |
|------|---------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 1 | **Merlot** | **≈ 44 %** of the total 110 800 ha planted | **Right‑Bank** – Libournais area (Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac, Côtes de Castillon) and the “Côtes de Bordeaux” hills. Merlot also dominates the “Bordeaux Supérieur” AOC on the right‑bank fringe. | Provides fruit‑forward colour, roundness and early‑drinking softness. |
| 2 | **Cabernet Sauvignon** | **≈ 30 %** | **Left‑Bank** – Médoc (including Haut‑Médoc, Saint‑Estèphe, Pauillac, Margaux), Graves and the “Bordeaux” AOC on the left‑bank plateau. Small plantings also exist in some Right‑Bank “Côtes de Bordeaux” sites, but the bulk is left‑bank. | Supplies structure, tannic backbone and ageing potential. |
| 3 | **Cabernet Franc** | **≈ 10 %** | **Both banks, but especially** the **Right‑Bank** (Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac) and the **Bordeaux Supérieur** area on the left‑bank fringe. It is also the dominant variety in the “Bordeaux AOC” red wines of the “Côtes de Bordeaux” and in the “Bordeaux‑Supérieur” AOC where it is often the second‑most‑planted red grape. | Adds aromatic finesse, acidity and herbaceous nuance; often used to soften very high‑Cabernet‑Sauvignon blends. |
| 4 | **Malbec** (locally called **Côt**) | **≈ 5 %** | **Right‑Bank “Côtes de Bordeaux”** (especially around Libourne and the “Bordeaux‑Supérieur” zone) and the **Médoc‑Graves border** where it is inter‑planted in small parcels for depth. | Historically a major component of “Bordeaux‑Supérieur” reds; today used in modest amounts to add colour and plum‑fruit richness. |
| 5 | **Petit Verdot** | **≈ 3 %** (the smallest of the five “classic” Bordeaux reds) | **Left‑Bank** – primarily the **Médoc** (especially Haut‑Médoc, Saint‑Estèphe) and **Graves** where it is planted on the best‑drained, sun‑exposed slopes. Very limited plantings are also found in the “Côtes de Bordeaux” on the right‑bank fringe. | Provides deep colour, strong tannins and a distinctive spicy‑pepper note; usually only 1–5 % of the blend. |

\* **Source** – 2022‑2023 vineyard‑area statistics published by the *Bordeaux Wine Council (Conseil Interprofessionnel du Vin de Bordeaux – CIVB)* and the French *Institut National de l’Origine et de la Qualité (INAO)*.  The percentages are calculated on the total vineyard surface (≈ 110 800 ha) that is officially classified as “Bordeaux” (red, white and rosé varieties combined).  Minor white varieties (Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle) are excluded because the question asks for the five most widely‑planted **grape varieties** overall; the five listed above account for roughly **92 %** of the entire planted area.

### Why each variety is concentrated in those sub‑regions

| Variety | Climate / soil advantage in its “home” sub‑region | Typical AOC examples |
|---------|---------------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Merlot** | Cool, clay‑rich soils of the Right‑Bank retain moisture, favouring Merlot’s early‑ripening nature. | Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac, Côtes de Castillon |
| **Cabernet Sauvignon** | Warm, gravelly, well‑drained soils of the Médoc and Graves accelerate phenolic development and preserve acidity. | Médoc, Haut‑Médoc, Pauillac, Graves, Sauternes (for the “white” component) |
| **Cabernet Franc** | Slightly cooler, limestone‑rich soils on the right‑bank and on the “Bordeaux‑Supérieur” plateau give the grape the acidity it needs. | Saint‑Émilion, Bordeaux‑Supérieur, Côtes de Bordeaux |
| **Malbec** | Historically planted on the deeper, more fertile soils of the Right‑Bank “Côtes de Bordeaux” where it can reach full ripeness without excessive heat. | Bordeaux‑Supérieur, Côtes de Bordeaux |
| **Petit Verdot** | Thrives on the best‑drained, sun‑exposed gravel of the Médoc’s “cru” sites, where its late‑ripening cycle can be completed. | Haut‑Médoc, Saint‑Estèphe, Graves |

### Quick reference chart

| Grape | % of total Bordeaux vines | Core area(s) | Typical AOC(s) where you’ll find it most |
|-------|---------------------------|--------------|------------------------------------------|
| Merlot | ~44 % | Right‑Bank (Libournais) | Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac |
| Cabernet Sauvignon | ~30 % | Left‑Bank (Médoc & Graves) | Médoc, Haut‑Médoc, Graves |
| Cabernet Franc | ~10 % | Right‑Bank & Bordeaux‑Supérieur | Saint‑Émilion, Bordeaux‑Supérieur |
| Malbec (Côt) | ~5 % | Right‑Bank “Côtes de Bordeaux” | Bordeaux‑Supérieur, Côtes de Bordeaux |
| Petit Verdot | ~3 % | Left‑Bank (Médoc/Graves) | Haut‑Médoc, Saint‑Estèphe, Graves |

---

**Take‑away:**  
- **Merlot** dominates the **Right‑Bank** and accounts for nearly half of all vines.  
- **Cabernet Sauvignon** is the backbone of the **Left‑Bank** classics.  
- **Cabernet Franc** bridges both banks but is especially important in **Saint‑Émilion** and **Bordeaux‑Supérieur** blends.  
- **Malbec** and **Petit Verdot** are “minor” but still essential to the traditional Bordeaux blend, each confined to a narrow strip of the region where the terroir suits their late‑ripening, high‑tannin profiles.  

These figures are the most recent official numbers (2022‑2023) and are widely cited by the CIVB, INAO and major Bordeaux trade publications.

### Why each variety is concentrated in those sub‑regions

| Variety | Climate / soil advantage in its “home” sub‑region | Typical AOC examples |
|---------|---------------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| **Merlot** | Cool, clay‑rich soils of the Right‑Bank retain moisture, favouring Merlot’s early‑ripening nature. | Saint‑Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac, Côtes de Castillon |
| **Cabernet Sauvignon** | Warm, gravelly, well‑drained soils of the Médoc and Graves accelerate phenolic development and preserve acidity. | Médoc, Haut‑Médoc, Pauillac, Graves |
| **Cabernet Franc** | Slightly cooler, limestone‑rich soils on the Right‑Bank and on the “Bordeaux‑Supérieur” plateau give the grape the acidity it needs. | Saint‑Émilion, Bordeaux‑Supérieur, Côtes de Bordeaux |
| **Malbec** | Historically planted on the deeper, more fertile soils of the Right‑Bank “Côtes de Bordeaux” where it can reach full ripeness without excessive heat. | Bordeaux‑Supérieur, Côtes de Bordeaux |
| **Petit Verdot** | Thrives on the best‑drained, sun‑exposed gravel of the Médoc’s “cru” sites, where its late‑ripening cycle can be completed. | Haut‑Médoc, Saint‑Estèphe, Graves |

**Take‑away:**  

- **Merlot** dominates the **Right‑Bank** and accounts for nearly half of all vines.  
- **Cabernet Sauvignon** is the backbone of the **Left‑Bank** classics.  
- **Cabernet Franc** bridges both banks but is especially important in **Saint‑Émilion** and **Bordeaux‑Supérieur** blends.  
- **Malbec** and **Petit Verdot** are “minor” but still essential to the traditional Bordeaux blend, each confined to narrow strips of the region where the terroir suits their late‑ripening, high‑tannin profiles.  

These figures are the most recent official numbers (2022‑2023) and are widely cited by the CIVB, INAO and major Bordeaux trade publications.
